posts.quote: THE SUNDAY SCHOOL FELT BOARD HAD ONE SHEEP THAT NEVER STAYED PUT, AND EVERY WEEK IT SLID RIGHT OFF THE EDGE.
posts.caption: Sunday school met in the church basement, in a room with a linoleum floor and a radiator that clanked all through the lesson. Mrs. Hadley kept her felt figures in a flour sack, and she pulled them out one at a time like a magician. There was a shepherd, a donkey, three kings in purple robes, and one little sheep that would not stay on the board. She would press it flat, go on with the story for another sentence, and down it would slide again. By the end of the year we were more interested in that sheep than in anything she said, and I suspect she knew it.
posts.first: Our teacher kept a tin of safety pins in the sack, and now and then she used one to hold that sheep up from behind. She never mentioned it, and we all pretended not to see. I still think that sheep taught me more about patience than the lesson did.

posts.quote: THE BANDSTAND SAT EMPTY ALL YEAR, AND THEN THE FOURTH OF JULY CAME AROUND AND IT WAS THE CENTER OF THE WORLD.
posts.caption: For fifty weeks of the year the bandstand in the town square was just a white wooden gazebo with peeling paint. Pigeons used it, and kids ran laps around the railing without anyone saying a word. Then the Fourth of July came around, the town council hung bunting from every post, and the high school band hauled their chairs up the steps. Suddenly it was the most important building in the county. By evening there were blankets spread on the grass clear to the edge of the square. The next morning somebody swept up the paper cups, and it went right back to being quiet.
posts.first: My grandfather played trombone in that band for thirty-one summers, and I never once heard him miss a note on the closing march. He kept his mouthpiece in his shirt pocket the rest of the year, and sometimes in January I'd catch him taking it out to look at it. I think that bandstand was where he kept his best days.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the brush salesman)
posts.quote: THE BRUSH SALESMAN / A SUITCASE OF SAMPLES, A FOOT IN THE DOOR, AND A FREE COMB FOR THE KIDS
posts.caption: He knocked on the screen door around ten in the morning, just after the breakfast dishes were done. The suitcase came open on the porch like a little store, with brushes for floors, brushes for bottles, and brushes for places you never knew needed one. Mom let him say his whole speech, because that was the polite thing to do, and then she bought the scrub brush she had been meaning to get anyway. The free comb went to whichever kid answered the door. He tipped his hat, thanked her for her time, and moved on to the Pattersons'. That was a whole day's work for him, one porch at a time.
posts.first: Ours came every spring for years, a quiet man in a gray suit who always remembered Mom's name and the dog's. She still had one of his vegetable brushes when she passed it down to me, with the bristles gone soft with age. I use it to this day.

posts.quote: The metronome ticked at one speed, I played at another, and my piano teacher never stopped smiling.
posts.first: Mrs. Albright kept a bowl of butterscotch candies on the piano and passed one over after every lesson, whether the lesson earned it or not. Nine years of lessons and I can play exactly two songs. I still hear that ticking whenever a room goes quiet.

posts.quote: DAD FISHED THE CREEK EVERY SATURDAY FOR TWENTY YEARS, AND WE NEVER ONCE ATE WHAT HE CAUGHT.
posts.caption: Every Saturday Dad was out the door before the sun, with a thermos, a folding stool, and a coffee can full of worms from the garden. He came back around noon smelling like creek water and sat down at the table looking perfectly satisfied. Mom would ask how he did, and he'd say it was a good morning, which could mean anything at all. In twenty years I can count on one hand the fish that made it into our skillet, and every one of them was small enough to feel sorry for. The truth was that nobody in our house wanted him to catch much, because the creek was the only place he ever sat still.
posts.first: I went along once when I was about nine. He handed me a pole, sat on his stool, and said exactly four words the whole morning. I have never been so relaxed in my life, and I didn't catch a thing either.

posts.quote: THE COAT WAS TWO SIZES TOO BIG, BECAUSE YOU WERE GOING TO GROW INTO IT BY SPRING.
posts.caption: Every October Mom took us to the store and bought the winter coat that was supposed to last. It was always a size or two bigger than you needed, with sleeves that covered your knuckles and a hem somewhere near your shins. She'd turn the cuffs back, pin them, and tell you to stand up straight. You wore it all winter looking like a small man in his father's overcoat. By March the sleeves were finally the right length, and by the next October she was letting the hem out for your little brother. Nothing in our house was ever bought for just one child.
posts.first: Mine was green wool with a hood that never stayed up. I can still see Mom kneeling in front of me with a mouthful of pins, turning the cuffs back one more time. I felt like I was wearing a tent, and I was proud of it.

posts.quote: THE PULL-DOWN MAP CAME DOWN LIKE A WINDOW SHADE, AND THE WHOLE WORLD WAS ON IT.
posts.caption: It lived rolled up above the chalkboard, and nobody noticed it until the teacher reached for the little ring on the bottom. Down it came with a rattle, and there was the whole world in faded pink and green and yellow. The oceans were the same pale blue all the way across, and the cracks in the paper ran right through the middle of the continents. She tapped the places with a wooden pointer while we tried not to look bored. Somebody always let it go too fast, and it snapped back up with a bang that woke half the room.
posts.first: Our teacher, Mr. Ellis, used to find our town on that map with the tip of his pointer and say it was right about there. It was a dot so small you could miss it, and he held the pointer on it anyway. I think that was the first time I understood where I lived.

posts.quote: THE SOAP BOX DERBY / A HOMEMADE CAR, A STEEP HILL, AND A PLAN YOUR FATHER HELPED YOU DRAW
posts.caption: It started with a drawing on the back of a feed sack, and Dad and I spent three Saturdays in the garage with a saw, a borrowed drill, and four wheels off an old wagon. The finished car looked more like a shoebox on wheels than a racer, but I thought it was beautiful. On race day the whole town lined the hill with folding chairs and lawn blankets. My car came in third out of five, and I walked back up that hill carrying it with a pride I have not felt since. Dad said nothing the whole way, then bought me a root beer at the corner store.
posts.first: Dad never had a plan for anything, but he had a pencil behind his ear that day and he measured every board twice. We painted it red because it was the only paint left in the garage. I still have the steering rope in a drawer somewhere.

posts.quote: DAD TESTED THE POND ICE WITH HIS BOOT FIRST, AND THEN WE ALL DECIDED TO TRUST HIM.
posts.caption: The first deep freeze of the winter, the whole neighborhood watched that pond like a pot on the stove. Nobody went near it until somebody's father walked out to the edge in his work boots. He stamped once, listened, then stamped again harder. If it cracked, we all groaned and went home for hot chocolate. If it held, there was a short nod, and every kid on the block was down at the pond with their skates tied together over one shoulder. By the end of the afternoon the ice looked like a map of everywhere we had been.
posts.first: My brother wore hand-me-down hockey skates a size too big, with two extra pairs of socks stuffed in the toes. He fell at least thirty times and was up laughing every time. The ice rang under us like a drum, and I still remember that sound.

posts.quote: OUR ROAD WAS GRAVEL, AND YOU COULD HEAR EVERY CAR COMING FROM A MILE AWAY.
posts.caption: On a quiet afternoon you heard it before you saw it, a low crunch that grew louder as the tires came closer. By the time the dust rose over the hill, Mom already knew whose car it was. She'd say it was the Hendersons or the mail truck, and she was never wrong. We learned to tell a pickup from a sedan by the sound alone, and we learned who was in a hurry by how much dust trailed behind. Nobody ever surprised us on that road. Nobody had to knock before they arrived, because the road announced them.
posts.first: My grandfather could tell you the make and year of every car on that road by the crunch alone. He sat on the porch steps with his coffee and named them off, one by one, before they came into view. He was right more often than he was wrong.
